title: Asking for a review
objectives: Open a pull request from a branch
Say which commits a pull request shows
Write a README with a results note that a stranger can check

screens.title: Asking for a review
screens.prose: A second pair of eyes catches the bug you cannot see. We will put a change on GitHub where a colleague can read it before it joins main.
You added a maximum drawdown function on a branch called `mdd`, short for maximum drawdown. Your colleague Sam should check it before it joins `main`. Both are on GitHub.

params.aria: Commit graph: each circle is a commit, each arrow points to the commit before it

state.caption: On GitHub: `main` on top, your branch `mdd` below

screens.question: Tap the commits Sam needs to read.

hints.text: Which commits are on `mdd` but not on `main`?
Main already has these.
Only D and E are new. A, B and C are on main already.

feedback.correct: D and E: the commits on the branch that main lacks.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sam only needs what main does not have yet.

byKey.all: You picked the whole history. A, B and C are on main already, so Sam has seen them.
byKey.newest: You picked only the newest. D is new too, and E builds on it.
byKey.with-base: C is where the branch starts, and it is already on main.

explain.text: D and E are on `mdd` and not on `main`. They are the whole change Sam must check. Everything before C is shared history.

screens.prose: On GitHub, a request to merge a branch into `main`, with room for comments, is a **pull request**. Here is how you would make one for the drawdown change.

params.aria: Commit graph: each circle is a commit, each arrow points to the commit before it

state.caption: On GitHub: `main` on top, your branch `mdd` below

screens.question: Put the steps in order.

lines.text: On GitHub, open a pull request from `mdd` into `main`

hints.text: Which step needs the branch to be on GitHub already?
Make the branch first, so the commit lands on it. Stage, commit, push the branch, then open the request.

feedback.correct: Branch, stage, commit, push, open the request.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step needs the one before it.

byKey.switch: Make the branch first, or the commit lands on main.
byKey.add: Stage the file after the branch exists and before the commit.
byKey.commit: The commit records what you staged, so it follows `git add`.
byKey.push: Push the branch once it holds your commit.
byKey.pr: GitHub can only show a branch it has. Open the request after the push.

explain.text: The branch keeps your change off `main`. Pushing it puts the branch on GitHub, where the request can point to it. The request then shows the commits on `mdd` that `main` lacks.

screens.prose: Sam comments: `max_drawdown` returns 0.34, but your docstring promises a negative number. You fix it on `mdd`, commit F and run `git push`.

params.aria: Commit graph: each circle is a commit, each arrow points to the commit before it

state.caption: On GitHub: `main` on top, your branch `mdd` below

screens.question: What happens to the pull request?

options.text: It now shows D, E and F; same request, same comments
You must open a new request for F
options.why: You treated the request as a snapshot. It follows the branch, so new commits appear in it.

options.text: F goes straight into `main`
options.why: You pushed to `mdd`, not `main`. Nothing reaches main until the request is merged.

options.text: Sam's comments are deleted
options.why: Comments stay on the request. GitHub marks old ones as outdated where the lines changed.

hints.text: Which branch did you push to?
The request shows this branch.
The request follows `mdd`, and F is now on `mdd`.

feedback.correct: The request follows the branch, so F joins it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A pull request shows whatever the branch holds now.

byKey.new: You expected a new request. The open one tracks `mdd`, so it picks up F by itself.

explain.text: The pull request points at the branch, not at fixed commits. Pushing F to `mdd` added it to the request. Sam can reply to the comment and read only the new commit.

screens.prose: While you waited, a colleague merged commit G into `main`: a fix to the data loader. Your branch still starts from C.

params.aria: Commit graph: each circle is a commit, each arrow points to the commit before it

state.caption: G is new on `main`; `mdd` starts from C

screens.question: Tap the commits your pull request shows now.

hints.text: Is G on your branch?
G is on main, not on `mdd`.
The request shows commits on `mdd` that `main` lacks. G is on main, so it is not among them.

feedback.correct: Still D, E and F. G is on main, not on your branch.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The request lists the branch's commits that main does not have.

byKey.with-g: You added G. G is on `main` and not on `mdd`, so it is not part of your change.
byKey.G: G is on `main`. Your request shows only what `mdd` adds.
byKey.C: C is shared by both, so it is not part of the change.

explain.text: Main moving on does not change what your branch adds: D, E and F. GitHub merges against the new main, so it checks that G and your work fit. If both edited the same lines, it reports a conflict to resolve first.

screens.prose: Sam also asks for a `README.md`, the page GitHub shows under the file list. A stranger should be able to run and check your project from it alone. Here is a draft.

columns: Draft README.md, one line per row
rows: # returns-project: returns, volatility and drawdown for one ETF
Results: SPY 2014 to 2023, volatility 17.6% a year, max drawdown −34.1%
Changes: every commit message since January
Ask Sam about the 2020 data gap

screens.question: Tap every line that belongs in the README.

hints.text: What does a stranger need to install, run and check the project?
This line must never be in any file on GitHub.
Keep what it is, how to install, run and test it, and the results. Drop the key, the history and private notes.

feedback.correct: What it is, how to install, run and test it, and what it found.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep only lines that help a stranger run and check the project.

byKey.no-results: You left out the results. The results note says what the code found, so a reader can check it.
byKey.no-tests: You left out how to run the tests. A reviewer runs them first.
byKey.r5c0: You kept the API key. Anyone who reads the page could use it, and it stays in the history.
byKey.r6c0: You kept the change list. `git log` holds that already, and it never goes stale.
byKey.r7c0: You kept a private note. Put questions for Sam in the pull request instead.

explain.text: A README answers four questions: what is this, how do I install it, how do I run it, how do I test it. The results note adds what it found, with the data and period. The key, the history and private notes belong elsewhere.

screens.prose:
Sam approves and clicks **Merge** on GitHub. Merge commit M joins `mdd` into `main` on origin. On your laptop you run:

```sh
$ git switch main
$ python returns.py data/spy.csv
```

params.aria: Commit graph: each circle is a commit, each arrow points to the commit before it

state.caption: `main` on your laptop (top) and on GitHub (bottom)

screens.question: Does your laptop's `main` include the drawdown function?

options.text: No, not until you run `git pull`
Yes: merging updated `main` everywhere
options.why: You expected the merge to reach your laptop. It happened on GitHub; your laptop changes only when you pull.

options.text: Yes, because your laptop has the `mdd` branch
options.why: You are on `main` now. The branch's commits are not in your local main until you pull M.

options.text: Never: merged work stays on GitHub
options.why: `git pull` brings M and everything it joined down to your laptop.

hints.text: Where did the merge happen?
M exists only on GitHub so far.
Your local `main` ends at G. Pull to fetch M and move main onto it.

feedback.correct: The merge happened on GitHub. Pull to bring it home.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare where M exists with where you are running the code.

byKey.yes: You expected the merge to update your laptop. GitHub cannot change your folder; you pull.

explain.text: M exists only on origin, so your local `main` still ends at G. `git pull` fetches M, with D, E and F behind it, and moves your main onto it. Then delete the old branch with `git branch -d mdd`.

screens.prose:
Here is the cycle you just ran:

```sh
$ git switch -c mdd             # one change, one branch
$ git commit ...                # as many commits as it needs
$ git push -u origin mdd        # the branch goes to GitHub
# GitHub: open a pull request, mdd into main
# review: fix, commit, git push (the request updates)
# GitHub: merge
$ git switch main
$ git pull                      # bring the merge home
```
screens.question: Sam asks for one more change after you opened the request. What do you do?

options.text: Commit it on `mdd` and push
Open a second pull request
options.why: You saw F join the open request by itself. A second request would split one change in two.

options.text: Commit it on `main` so Sam sees it at once
options.why: That skips the review the request exists for.

options.text: Close the request and start again
options.why: Closing throws away the discussion. The request follows the branch, so just push.

hints.text: What happened when you pushed F?
The open request picked up F because it follows the branch.

feedback.correct: Push to the branch; the request follows it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think back to commit F.

explain.text: A pull request tracks a branch. Each push to that branch updates it, and the discussion stays in one place. Main changes only at the merge.

screens.prose: From item 1.2 on, every project goes on GitHub with a README, a test and a results note. Your Stage 1 project reads daily SPY closes and reports volatility and maximum drawdown. A reader should be able to rerun it and get the same numbers.

options.text: `python returns.py data/spy.csv` on SPY daily closes, 2 Jan 2014 to 29 Dec 2023: volatility 17.6% a year, max drawdown −34.1% (19 Feb to 23 Mar 2020).
The strategy works well and the drawdown is small.
options.why: You gave a verdict with no numbers. A reader has nothing to check.

options.text: Max drawdown −34.1%.
options.why: You gave a number without the data, the period or the command. A reader cannot reproduce it.

options.why: A reader on GitHub cannot open your laptop. The note must be in the repository.

hints.text: What would you need to get the same number yourself?
You need the command, the data and its period, and the numbers to compare against.

feedback.correct: Command, data, period and numbers: enough to rerun and compare.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the note a reader could check by running the code.

byKey.bare: You gave the number alone. Without the data and period, a different answer proves nothing.

explain.text: A results note is a claim someone else can test: the command, the data, the dates and the numbers. Drawdown on these dates is a fall from 338.34 to 222.95. Anyone who reruns it should see −34.1%.

ideas: A pull request asks to merge a branch into main. It shows the commits the branch has and main lacks.
The request follows the branch: push more commits and it updates.
A README says what the project is and how to install, run and test it. Its results note gives the command, data, period and numbers.

formula.name: What a pull request shows
formula.note: New commits on main do not join it.

summary.trap: Merging on GitHub does not change your laptop. Switch to main and pull.

quiz.prose: `main` has commits A, B, C. You branched from B and made X and Y.
quiz.question: Which commits does your pull request show?

options.text: X and Y
B, X and Y
options.why: B is where the branch starts. It is on main already.

options.text: C, X and Y
options.why: C is on main, not on your branch.

options.text: A, B, X and Y
options.why: You listed the branch's whole history. Main has A and B already.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drop everything main already has.

explain.text: Your branch holds A, B, X and Y. Main holds A, B and C. The request shows what the branch adds: X and Y.

quiz.prose: You open a pull request with 2 commits. Review takes three rounds, and you push one new commit each round.
quiz.question: How many commits does the request show at the end?

widget.label: Commits in the request
widget.accept: 5: the 2 you opened with, plus 3 pushed later.

feedback.correct: 2 + 3 = 5. Each push adds to the same request.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Every commit pushed to the branch joins the request.

byKey.two: You kept only the first two. Commits pushed later join the same request.
byKey.three: You counted only the review commits. The first two are still there.

explain.text: The request follows the branch. Each round's commit joins it, so it ends with 2 + 3 = 5. Reviewers can read the whole set, or only the newest.

quiz.prose: A README reads: what the project does; `pip install -r requirements.txt`; `python returns.py data/spy.csv`; and the results for SPY, 2014 to 2023.
quiz.question: What is it missing?

options.text: How to run the tests
A list of every commit
options.why: `git log` holds the history already.

options.text: The API key for the data
options.why: Keys never go in any committed file. Say how to set one instead.

options.text: Nothing: it is complete
options.why: A reviewer runs the tests first, and this README does not say how.

feedback.correct: A line such as `pytest`, so a reader can check the code works.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run through install, run, test, results.

explain.text: The four questions are what, install, run and test. This README answers three, plus the results. Add `pytest`, with a word on what the tests check.

quiz.prose: Your pull request was merged on GitHub an hour ago. On your laptop, `git log` on `main` does not show it.
quiz.question: Why?

options.text: You have not pulled since the merge
The merge failed
options.why: GitHub showed it as merged. The merge is there; your laptop has not fetched it.

options.text: `git log` only shows branches, not merges
options.why: `git log` shows merge commits like any other. This one is not on your laptop yet.

options.text: You forgot to push after the merge
options.why: The merge happened on GitHub. There is nothing of yours to push.

feedback.correct: Merges on GitHub reach your laptop when you pull.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask where the merge commit exists.

explain.text: The merge commit exists on origin only. `git pull` on main brings it down. Until then your local main is an hour behind.
